Dublin. The capital and largest city of Ireland, situated on the River Liffey's mouth at the Irish Sea, with a population of over one point two million in the metropolitan area. A city of Georgian architecture, literary giants, and intellectual ferment, Dublin has been the center of Irish culture, politics, and commerce since medieval times.

Dublin was founded by Vikings in the ninth century at the confluence of the River Liffey and the Poddle. Its name derives from Dubh Linn, meaning black pool. Trinity College Dublin, founded in fifteen ninety-two, is Ireland's oldest university and remains one of Europe's most prestigious institutions. It houses the illuminated manuscript Book of Kells. Dublin was the center of the Irish independence movement. James Joyce, Samuel Beckett, William Butler Yeats, and Oscar Wilde all emerged from Dublin's literary scene and profoundly influenced world literature.

The city's Georgian architecture, particularly around Merrion Square and the Liffey Quays, makes it one of the finest eighteenth-century urban landscapes in Europe. The Irish Famine from eighteen forty-five to eighteen fifty-two devastated Ireland, causing mass starvation and emigration. Dublin, as the capital, was a focal point of the crisis and its aftermath. Dublin was the seat of Irish Home Rule agitation in the late nineteenth century and the epicenter of the Easter Rising in nineteen sixteen, which sparked the Irish War of Independence and eventually Ireland's independence.

The Guinness Storehouse and the city's famous pub culture reflect Dublin's role as a social and cultural hub. Guinness beer was first brewed there in seventeen fifty-nine. James Joyce's modernist novel Ulysses, set entirely in Dublin on June sixteenth, nineteen zero four, is considered one of the greatest novels ever written. The date is now commemorated as Bloomsday.
